newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai banks face toughest time in years.
newsitem.headline: Thai banks face toughest time in years.

text.p: Several Thai banks face the prospect of lower profits for the first time in a decade as tougher provision requirements and loan exposure to an ailing property sector hit margins, analysts said on Tuesday.

They projected eight big and medium Thai banks, out of a total of 15, would see their 1997 earnings decline an average three percent against about seven percent growth in 1996 and 15 percent growth in 1995.
The lower bank profits would be the first in more than 10 years, and small banks would fare worse than big ones, they added.
"Banks have been hard hit by the property crisis, partly due to over-stretched exposure," said a foreign analyst who declined to be named.

The central Bank of Thailand added to the gloom of commercial banks last week, ordering them to set aside another 15 percent in provisions for sub-standard assets on top of 100 percent reserves for doubtful and non-performing debts.
It told banks to meet the higher provision requirement, estimated at 24 billion baht ($930 million), within two years, half of it in the next 12 months.
In 1996, Thai banks extended about 10 percent of their total loans to property developers who reeled under their fourth year of a business slump with no immediate recovery in sight.
But they carried a lighter burden than finance companies which tied a quarter of their loans to the sector, prompting panic among investors last week and huge withdrawals.
Analysts said about 800 billion baht of bank and finance company loans were in the property sector.

An analyst at Krungthai Thanakit Plc estimated that at least 8.8 percent of bank loans should be booked as non-performing against 12 percent for finance firms. "These are very conservative estimates by any definition," he said.

Another analyst said about 2.00-3.00 percent of total loans of Bangkok Bank Plc and Thai Farmers Bank Plc were non-performing, against about 8.5 percent for Krung Thai Bank Plc and nearly 10 percent for Thai Military Bank Plc.

Analyst Andrew Maude at Vickers Ballas Research said big banks, especially Bangkok Bank and Thai Farmers, could easily handle the tougher provision requirements, having already met them before the central bank instruction last week.
But analysts said the burden would be felt hard by medium and small banks. One said Thai Military would need to set aside about three billion baht provision for sub-standard assets.

They said decisions by Moody's Investors Service to downgrade short-term debt ratings of Thai banks last October and its current review of their long-term ratings had raised foreign funding costs of Thai banks by almost 100 basis points since the last quarter of 1996.
Maude at Vickers Ballas forecast that the average net interest margin of eight top Thai banks would be squeezed to 3.65 percentage points this year from 3.90 in 1996.

Analysts projected that Bangkok Bank, the biggest Thai bank, would post 3.00-6.00 percent net profit growth this year against 5.3 percent in 1996. Thai Farmers' net profit would grow 2.00-4.00 percent, up from 2.5 percent growth a year ago.
But they expected falls at Krung Thai and Thai Military, buy 11 percent and 19 percent respectively.
